tagline.text: A healing shrine reached by climbing 300-odd steps above Lucban

location.label: Location
location.text: Barangay Tinamnan, Lucban, Quezon, along the Lucban–Tayabas Road

best_season.label: Best time to visit
best_season.text: December–May dry season (Holy Week and Pahiyas are crowded)

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱300–1,500 (per person, local costs only, excluding round-trip public transport from Manila)

children.text: Kamay ni Hesus Shrine is a Catholic pilgrimage site on the slopes of Mount Banahaw in Lucban, Quezon. It is known for the statue of Christ, about 50 feet tall, at the top of 300-odd steps, the Stations of the Cross sculptures, and its Healing Masses, and millions of people visit during Holy Week.

Kamay ni Hesus means "the hand of Jesus" in Tagalog. The official name is Kamay ni Hesus Healing Church, and it stands in Barangay Tinamnan, about a 15-minute drive from Lucban town along the Lucban–Tayabas Road. Set on a hill at the foot of Mount Banahaw and a little over 100 km from Manila, it is counted among the most visited Catholic pilgrimage sites in the Philippines. Locals often shorten the name of the Way of the Cross grotto to simply "the Grotto."

The shrine was founded by Fr. Joseph "Joey" Faller. According to Wikipedia, construction began in February 2002 and finished in 2004, paid for with donations and an inheritance the priest received. The grounds started at about 5 hectares and have since grown to about 7 hectares. It belongs to the Diocese of Lucena, and pilgrims increased as the priest became widely known for leading Healing Masses. The shrine closed in 2020 and 2021 because of COVID-19 and reopened in 2022, and in November 2022 a new building known as the "Healing Dome" (Healing Church of the Risen Christ) was completed.

The part that impresses most visitors is the Way of the Cross up the hill. Roughly 300 concrete steps lead from the grotto at the bottom to the summit, and life-size sculptures of the 14 Stations of the Cross line the path. At the top stands a statue of the Risen Christ with open arms, about 50 feet (about 15 m) tall, where pilgrims touch the base and pray. The ascending and descending paths are separate, so the flow of people is said not to jam even when it is busy. In the gardens at the foot of the hill, scenes from the Bible such as a Noah's Ark replica, the Garden of Eden and a Sea of Galilee have been set up, so families on pilgrimage can stay a long while.

This guide is for travelers who want to visit Lucban from Manila on a day trip or half-day trip. Entry is free because it is a religious site, but modest dress and respectful behavior are expected. During Holy Week (the week before Easter) millions of people arrive and the place becomes completely different from usual, so decide which experience you want before you plan. A weekday morning suits a quiet climb, and a day with a Healing Mass suits those who want to feel the pilgrimage atmosphere. Fees and Mass times change often, so check the shrine's official Facebook page or call for the latest information.

About 300 steps run from the grotto to the summit, and sources count them slightly differently, at 305, 310 and so on. Life-size sculptures of the 14 Stations line the route, and many pilgrims walk slowly and meditate along the way. Out of courtesy, keep conversation low and walk quietly while going up.
At the top of the hill stands a statue of Christ with open arms, about 50 feet (about
) tall. Pilgrims place a hand at its foot and pray, and from the summit you can look out over the Lucban area.
This is the event that made the shrine most famous. Several sources say Healing Masses are held on Wednesdays and Saturdays at
, but the schedule differs slightly between sources and changes with the season and special events. The church fills up early on Healing Mass days, so arrive at least 30 minutes before it starts.

Completed in November 2022, this large domed building serves as the shrine's new main church. The older healing chapel holds about 1,000 people, and a 2019 report said more than 5,000 worshippers showed up and spilled outside the building. Avoid photography and flash during Mass.

blocks.title: Noah's Ark and the Garden of Eden

children.text: The gardens at the foot of the hill hold outdoor displays that recreate Bible stories. The Noah's Ark replica also serves as lodging and a retreat facility for pilgrims, and the Garden of Eden has Adam and Eve, animal sculptures, fountains and a small playground. It is a good place to rest with children.

Near the grotto exit is a level rosary-prayer area with life-size sculptures of the Joyful, Sorrowful and Glorious Mysteries. It is an alternative path for older visitors or anyone whose knees make the stairs hard.

On the night of Good Friday, many pilgrims continue the "Alay Lakad" tradition of walking about 24 km from Lucena to Lucban to reach the shrine. The Inquirer reported more than 6 million visitors during Holy Week 2025, and roads are practically gridlocked at that time. This is a walk of faith, not a spectacle, so it calls for respect.

Around the entrance and in nearby shops you can buy Lucban specialties such as longganisa sausage, pancit habhab noodles, broas, cassava chips and otap, along with rosaries and candles. After the climb, local snacks are a good way to recover, and they are popular as gifts.

items.title: Half-day course
items.subtitle: Climbing the steps and strolling the gardens

children.text: Arrive at the shrine entrance from Lucban town by tricycle or car. On weekends the parking lot starts to fill before this time.
Climb the Way of the Cross steps from the grotto below. Rest at the 14 Stations along the way and continue up to the statue of Christ at the summit. Allow about
40–60 minutes
at a slow pace.
On a Wednesday or Saturday, attend the Healing Mass. On other days, look around the gardens and Noah's Ark.
Walk through the Garden of Eden, the Sea of Galilee area and Rosary Hill, then buy longganisa and rosaries at the souvenir shops.
Have lunch with pancit habhab at a restaurant near the shrine or in Lucban town.
The stairs are very hard in the midday heat, so climb early in the morning. Mass times vary by day of the week, so check before you visit.

items.title: Full-day Lucban course
items.subtitle: The shrine, the town church and local food

children.text: Arrive in Lucban by bus or car from Manila, passing through Lucena.
Climb the steps and stroll the gardens, and join a Mass if the timing works.
Return to Lucban town for a meal of pancit habhab and longganisa.
Visit the San Luis Obispo de Tolosa Parish Church and the plaza in town.
Head back to Lucena or Manila to match your bus times. Getting home after dark is harder, so leave in good time.
Buses to Lucena Grand Terminal (JAM Liner, JAC Liner and others) leave from EDSA Kamuning, Buendia–Taft, Araneta Center Cubao and other points in Manila. The trip takes about
3–4 hours
, and one guide gives the fare as about ₱190–225. Fares change, so confirm locally.
At Lucena Terminal, board a jeepney or minivan (modern jeepney) to Lucban. Fares differ between sources, ranging from ₱25 to ₱57, and a 2026 local account gives about ₱57. The ride takes about
45–60 minutes
. Tell the driver "Kamay ni Hesus" and he will drop you at the junction by the shrine entrance. Modern jeepneys sometimes take the bypass road instead of entering the town.
Bus schedules and fares vary by operator and change greatly during Holy Week. Check the latest information before you leave.
You can also take a bus from Manila to Santa Cruz (Laguna) in about
2 hours
, then a jeepney through Pagsanjan, Cavinti and Luisiana to Lucban. This route has long stretches and adds about
1 hour 30 minutes
Take SLEX and exit at Santo Tomas (Batangas), then drive through San Pablo, Tiaong, Candelaria, Sariaya and Tayabas into Lucban. The trip takes about
3–4 hours
. This road is congested during Holy Week and on weekends.
One guide puts round-trip tolls and fuel at about ₱800–1,200, but this depends on the vehicle, so treat it as a rough guide only.

From the plaza in Lucban town, a tricycle is the easiest way to reach the shrine. Fares are quoted at about ₱15–30 per person. Tell the driver "Grotto" and he will understand. Parking at the shrine is about ₱30–100 for a car, and varies widely by period.
Because you climb steps on foot, the cooler, drier months are best. The easiest time is a weekday morning from
to
, and some reviews say Saturdays are quieter than Sundays.

Avoid Holy Week (the week before Easter) and the Lucban Pahiyas Festival on May 15, when road closures and crowds make getting around hard. If you want to see the pilgrimage atmosphere, you could consider weekdays in the weeks before Easter (Lent).

Most visitors come as a day trip from Manila, but to attend an early-morning Mass you can also stay the night before in Lucban or Lucena. Noah's Ark inside the shrine is said to have air-conditioned rooms for pilgrims and retreat visitors. Reservations and rates must be asked of the shrine directly, and the main phone number is +63 42 540 2206. Check availability and rates before your visit.

Food here centers on Lucban specialties. Pancit habhab is a stir-fried noodle dish with almost no broth, sold at restaurants in town and shops in front of the shrine, and longganisa is a small, strongly garlicky sausage. Broas, cassava chips and otap are also popular as gifts. There are also a food court and snack shops inside the shrine, so top up on water and snacks after the climb. If hygiene concerns you, pick a busy stall.
Dress modestly, covering the shoulders, and avoid shorts above the knee and sleeveless tops. You can be turned back at the entrance for your clothing.
The steps are steep and the sun is strong, so wear sneakers with non-slip soles and avoid sandals and slippers. Bring at least one bottle of water per person.
The church fills up early on Healing Mass days (mainly Wednesday and Saturday mornings). Arrive at least
30 minutes
before Mass begins.
Do not use flash during Mass, and step aside so you do not block anyone praying on the Way of the Cross.
Carry small bills (₱20, ₱50, ₱100) to pay for tricycles, donations and snacks easily.
On weekends and holidays the parking lot fills before
, so go early.
The steps are hard for wheelchair users and people with limited mobility. Walking Rosary Hill is an alternative.
In the rainy season (
June–October
), bring a raincoat or umbrella, and on sunny days you need a hat and sunscreen.

During Holy Week (especially around Good Friday) millions of people arrive, roads gridlock and entry times change. Avoid this period if you can, and if you go, be sure to check the latest announcements.
Opening hours differ by source: some list
on weekdays and
on Wednesday, Saturday and Sunday, while others list
daily. The grotto and upper sections may close at
, so arrive by 3 PM at the latest.
During Holy Week bags are inspected and police are posted. Pack light and do not bring sharp objects such as knives.
In crowded areas, beware of pickpockets and lost phones. Keep valuables in front of you.
The steps can be too much for people with heart or knee problems. It is fine to rest halfway or turn back.
During construction or events some areas may be closed, and Mass schedules change. Check the latest announcements.
About
15 minutes
by car from the shrine, the town of
Lucban
is known for the Pahiyas Festival on May 15 and the San Luis Obispo parish church.
The old town right next to Lucban,
Tayabas
still has Spanish-era churches and a bridge, so it combines well with a Lucban trip.
Villa Escudero
is a plantation resort famous for lunch under a waterfall, and it is in the same province of Quezon as Lucban.
The capital of Quezon,
Lucena
is the transfer point for buses from Manila, and a handy place to eat or shop on the way back.
